ddx.step1_summary: - Chief complaint: 26-year-old Adriana with a headache for about 3 days. Location: mainly around the right eye, but feels like it involves the whole head. Nature: dull most of the time with episodic sharpness. Severity: ~8/10. Temporal pattern: gradually worsening over 3 days; present most of the time, but fluctuating in intensity. Aggravating/relieving: worsened by light; NSAID (ibuprofen) used for 2 days without meaningful relief. No vomiting. - Associated symptoms: photophobia (light hurts), nausea/sick feeling, neck stiffness; no focal neurological deficits reported (no weakness, no speech difficulty), no vision loss reported, no fever, no rash. Difficulty focusing at work. - Onset/context: symptoms began at work, persisted through the next day, worsened upon waking. - Past medical history: history of headaches; no prior migraine diagnosis; family history positive for migraines (mother and sister). Regular meds: none. Allergies: none known. - Social history: lives with three housemates, works in IT (high screen time, high mental workload, stress related to new project), social smoker and social drinker. Eye history: wearing glasses since age 5; no recent eye test. - Physical exam details: not provided in transcript (no vitals or detailed neuro/eye exam documented). - Labs/imaging: none mentioned.

V: Migraine (without aura or with aura considered) – fits: unilateral around eye, photophobia, nausea, progressive daily headache over days, family history of migraines.
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) – fits as a consideration in a young woman with persistent, focal headache; presents without fever or focal deficits but can be subtle.

Intracranial hemorrhage/subarachnoid hemorrhage – less likely given gradual progression over 3 days and absence of thunderclap pain, but included as a vascular cause to consider in ongoing evaluation.
I: Meningitis/encephalitis – neck stiffness and photophobia with severe headache could reflect meningeal irritation; however, absence of fever or altered mental status lowers probability.
Acute sinusitis – can cause unilateral facial/eye-area pain with headache, but typically with facial fullness or purulent nasal symptoms.
Optic neuritis – can cause eye pain and photophobia, though typically with visual changes; currently patient reports no vision loss.
N: Brain tumor or intracranial mass – could present with progressive headache; less likely given only 3 days of symptoms, but included as a possibility in broader differential.
Precocious or unrelated intracranial pathology (e.g., abscess) – less likely but within broad neoplastic/infectious considerations.
D: Tension-type headache – can present with dull, diffuse head pain and stress-related triggers (work stress, screen time); may be less likely given prominent photophobia and nausea.
Dehydration-related headache – possible contributor given symptoms and work conditions, though not strongly supported by history.
I2: Medication-overuse headache (MOH) – history of taking ibuprofen regularly (three tablets per day) for a couple of days; MOH can occur with frequent acute meds, though short use makes this less certain.
Caffeine withdrawal headache – possible if there is irregular caffeine intake, not confirmed in transcript.
C: Chiari malformation or other congenital intracranial/anatomical predisposition – less likely but could be considered in atypical or non-responsive headaches.
A: Autoimmune/Inflammatory vascular processes (less likely) – included as a broad category in case of inflammatory etiologies; not strongly supported by current data.
T: Traumatic (post-traumatic) headache – not suggested by history (no head injury reported).
E: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) – in a young adult; would typically require features like papilledema and obesity; not currently described, but considered in broad differential for persistent headaches.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Migraine (without aura) with possible genetic predisposition
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Most consistent with the triplet of unilateral/right-eye–predominant pain, gradual onset over 3 days, photophobia, nausea, and history of migraines in close relatives. The current lack of clear aura does not exclude migraine. Past improvement with NSAIDs in the past supports a primary headache pattern that responds to analgesics. Family history strengthens probability.
supporting_evidence: Pain around right eye with head-to-head involvement
Gradual escalation over 3 days with persistent daily symptoms
Family history of migraines (mother and sister)
opposing_evidence: No vomiting and no clear focal neurological deficits
Response to ibuprofen was inadequate this time (but dose/response may vary)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Could explain dull, diffuse head pain with stress/work-related factors and high screen time; however, photophobia and nausea are less typical for tension-type headaches, which makes migraine more likely in this case.

opposing_evidence: Prominent photophobia (pain with bright lights) and nausea favor migraine over tension-type

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Meningitis/encephalitis (less likely but must remain on differential)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Repeated NSAID use can contribute to MOH. The patient has used ibuprofen for 2 days at a relatively high frequency; this could worsen or maintain headaches in some scenarios, though MOH typically requires more prolonged use.
supporting_evidence: Ibuprofen taken three times daily for two days
Patient seeking stronger analgesia due to lack of relief
opposing_evidence: MOH usually develops with more prolonged use; data here are limited to a few days
